definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self: it cannot be an object of thought (2.25, with 'unmanifest' and 'unchangeable').

literal: non-dharma, what is contrary to dharma

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, the disorder that overpowers a family once its family dharmas perish, leading to the corruption of its women and varṇa-mixture (1.40–41).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.47: one's right or proper claim, which extends to action alone and never to its fruits.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the compound adhyātma-cetas (3.30): the mind directed to the self, with which one resigns all actions to Kṛṣṇa; commentators gloss it variously.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense of 'I' by which one whose self is deluded thinks 'I am the doer', though actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); the one who attains peace is without it (nirahaṃkāra, 2.71).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self: unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval (2.20); knowing it as unborn one sees that it neither slays nor is slain (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Inaction: one should not be attached to it (2.47); action is better than inaction, and without action even the body cannot be maintained (3.8).

notes: The Gītā returns to action and inaction at 4.16–18 (outside this chunk).

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.15 the imperishable from which brahman arises (in the chain: action from brahman, brahman from the imperishable); its identification is disputed among commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The goal for which the steadfast person, unmoved by the contacts of the senses and the same in pleasure and pain, is fit (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The contacts of the senses with their objects, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go and are impermanent; they are to be endured (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the cycle of 3.14: beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice.

literal: immeasurable; not an object of the means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the eternal, indestructible embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The manner of action taught in chapter 3: the karma-yogin acts unattached (3.7); one should always perform the action to be done unattached, thereby reaching the highest (3.19); the wise act unattached for the holding together of the world (3.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.16: what is not (the non-existent or unreal), of which there is no being (bhāva); what exactly is meant is disputed among commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping (anasūyantaḥ) are freed from actions (3.31); those who carp at it and do not follow it are lost (3.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna calls the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra ātatāyinaḥ, and says sin would come upon them for killing even these aggressors (1.36).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self in which the one of steady wisdom is content — in the self alone, by the self (2.55) — and in which one who has nothing to do delights and is satisfied (3.17); knowing what is beyond the understanding (which 3.42 calls only 'he', saḥ; the commentators take it as the self), one steadies the self by the self (ātmānam ātmanā, 3.43). Also used reflexively and for one's person, nature or mind (vidheyātmā 2.64; vimūḍhātmā 3.6, 3.27; ātmavān 2.45; kāmātmānaḥ 2.43). The embodied one of 2.12–30 is called dehin or śarīrin, not ātman.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The condition of the person who delights in, is satisfied in and content in the self alone, for whom nothing remains to be done and who depends on no being for any purpose (3.17–18).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: That by which all this is pervaded is indestructible (2.17); the knower knows the embodied one as indestructible (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one is called unmanifest (2.25); beings have an unmanifest beginning and end and are manifest only in the middle (2.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of that by which all this is pervaded, which no one can destroy (2.17), and of the self known as indestructible and unborn (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the unyoked lack; without it there is no peace (2.66). Commentators gloss it as steady contemplation, dwelling on the self, or conviction.

notes: Glossed by the commentators as meditation or as intent absorption in knowledge of the self.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Beings, whose beginning and end are unmanifest and middle manifest (2.28), and who arise from food (3.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What one attains who abides in the brahmic state even at the time of death (2.72); first use of the term in the text.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.72 in the compounds brāhmī sthiti and brahmanirvāṇa (the state and goal of the one of steady wisdom). In 3.15 'brahma' arises from the imperishable and is the source of action, and the 'all-pervading brahman' is established in sacrifice; commentators take brahma in 3.15 as the Veda or as prakṛti.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.46 the 'knowing brāhmaṇa', for whom all the Vedas are of as much use as a well amid a flood.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The state of the one of steady wisdom described in 2.55–71; having attained it one is no longer deluded, and abiding in it even at death one attains brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The understanding declared 'according to sāṃkhya' and 'according to yoga', joined with which one casts off the bondage of action (2.39); when resolute it is single, when irresolute many-branched (2.41); it must cross the thicket of delusion and stand immovable in samādhi (2.52–53); it is destroyed after the loss of memory (2.63) and becomes steady in serenity (2.65); higher than the mind (3.42) and one of the seats of desire (3.40). Arjuna asks why action is urged if buddhi is superior (3.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The discipline of action yoked with understanding: action is far inferior to it (2.49); yoked with it one casts off good and evil deeds (2.50) and the wise, abandoning the fruit of action, are freed from the bondage of birth (2.51); introduced as the 'yoga' form of the teaching at 2.39.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the wise should not cause in the ignorant who are attached to action (3.26; cf. 3.29 'should not unsettle').
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The bodies of the eternal embodied one have an end (2.18); in this body come childhood, youth, old age, and so another body (2.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The one who dwells in the body: passes through the ages of life and into another body (2.13); casts off worn-out bodies as one casts off clothes (2.22); is eternally unslayable in everyone's body (2.30); objects turn away from it when it does not feed on them (2.59); desire deludes it by covering knowledge (3.40).

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably for the embodied one in BhG 2.13–30.
The dehin of 2.12–30 is what the commentators call the ātman; the chunk itself uses ātman for the self in 2.55, 3.17, 3.43.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The gods, nourished by sacrifice, nourish human beings in turn and give the enjoyments they desire (3.11–12).

literal: that which upholds; right order, duty

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The field of the battle is the 'field of dharma' (1.1). In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas and the dharmas of the birth-group perish when a family is destroyed, and adharma prevails (1.40–43); he is bewildered about dharma (2.7). Kṛṣṇa speaks of svadharma: for a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (dharmya, 2.31, 2.33); one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's (3.35); even a little of 'this dharma' (the yoga of understanding) protects from great fear (2.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast one is not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); the steadfast one, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); the steady-minded is not agitated in sorrows (2.56); in serenity all sorrows cease (2.65).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: With rāga, set in each sense towards its object — a waylayer not to be yielded to (3.34); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); the one of steady wisdom neither rejoices nor hates (2.57).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act helplessly (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas, and the deluded think 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower thinks 'the guṇas move among the guṇas' (3.28); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain, and Arjuna is to be free of them (2.45); desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's venerable elders (Bhīṣma, Droṇa), whom he would rather not kill even if it meant living on alms (2.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The senses are to be withdrawn from their objects like a tortoise's limbs (2.58); they are turbulent and carry off the mind even of the wise (2.60, 2.67); they are to be restrained (2.61, 2.68) and controlled first when fighting desire (3.41); rāga and dveṣa are set in each sense towards its object (3.34); they are one of the seats of desire (3.40); the senses are high, the mind higher (3.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The objects from which the senses are to be withdrawn (2.58, 2.68), on which the hypocrite dwells in mind (3.6), and in which attraction and aversion are set (3.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The bondage from which the wise, yoked with understanding and abandoning the fruit of action, are freed (2.51).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dharmas of the birth-group which, with the family dharmas, Arjuna says are uprooted by the faults of family-destroyers (1.43).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Knowledge is covered by desire, the constant enemy of the knower (3.38–40); desire is the destroyer of knowledge and realization (jñāna-vijñāna, 3.41); those who carp at Kṛṣṇa's teaching are deluded about all knowledge (3.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The commitment (niṣṭhā) of the sāṃkhyas, one of the two taught by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire: the ritual-minded are 'desire-souled' (2.43); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires that enter the mind (2.55, 2.71) and is entered by desires like the ocean without being moved (2.70); desire is born of attachment and gives rise to anger (2.62); named with anger as the enemy born of rajas that covers knowledge, seated in the senses, mind and understanding, to be slain (3.37–43).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action: one's entitlement is to it, never to its fruits (2.47); mere action is far inferior to buddhiyoga (2.49); no one remains without acting even for a moment (3.5); action is better than inaction (3.8); it binds except when done for sacrifice (3.9); sacrifice arises from action and action from brahman (3.14–15); done unattached it leads to the highest (3.19); Janaka and others reached perfection by it (3.20); all actions are done by the guṇas (3.27) and are to be renounced in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Cast off by one joined with the understanding according to yoga (2.39); the world is bound by action (karmabandhana) except for action done for sacrifice (3.9); the wise joined with understanding are freed from the bondage of birth (janmabandha, 2.51).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The commitment of the yogins, one of the two declared by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3); undertaken with the organs of action by one who controls the senses with the mind and is unattached (3.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fruit of action, to which one has no right and which should not be one's motive (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are wretched (2.49); the wise abandon the fruit born of action (2.51); the ritual-minded's speech offers birth as the fruit of action (2.43).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Restraining the organs of action while recalling objects in the mind is hypocrisy (3.6); karmayoga is undertaken with the organs of action, the senses controlled by the mind (3.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fault (kārpaṇya-doṣa) by which Arjuna says his very nature is struck when he asks for instruction (2.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One deluded by ahaṃkāra thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); Kṛṣṇa says that by not acting he would be the doer (cause) of confusion (3.24).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dejection that has come upon Arjuna at the critical moment, not practised by the noble, not leading to heaven, bringing disgrace (2.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.50 yoga is defined as 'skill in actions' (karmasu kauśalam).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The unmanliness to which Arjuna is told not to yield, with 'petty weakness of heart' (hṛdaya-daurbalya) (2.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Anger: arises from desire and gives rise to delusion (2.62–63); the sage of steady thought is free from it (2.56); named with desire as the enemy born of rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The supreme compassion that overcame Arjuna on seeing his kinsmen (1.28, 2.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pitiable are those whose motive is the fruit of action (2.49).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: For a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma (2.31); happy the kṣatriyas who meet such a battle, an open door to heaven (2.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The destruction of a family, whose fault Arjuna says the greedy Kauravas do not see but he does (1.38–39); it destroys the family dharmas (1.40).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument the eternal family dharmas perish when a family is destroyed (1.40), are uprooted by the family-destroyers (1.43), and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell (1.44).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The Kauravas' minds are overcome by greed (1.38); Arjuna laments being ready to kill his own people out of greed for the pleasures of kingship (1.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The holding together of the world, with a view to which one should act (3.20) and the wise act unattached (3.25), since people follow the standard the best person sets (3.21).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The turbulent senses carry away the mind (2.60), and the mind following the roving senses carries away wisdom (2.67); recalling objects in the mind while restraining the organs of action is hypocrisy (3.6); the senses are controlled by the mind in karmayoga (3.7); higher than the senses, lower than the understanding (3.42); a seat of desire (3.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa's teaching (me matam), which those who follow with faith are released from actions and those who cavil at are lost (3.31–32).

literal: having me as the highest; intent on me

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa, having restrained all the senses (2.61).

literal: contact of the senses (with their objects)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sense-contacts give cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go, are impermanent, and are to be endured (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits recalling sense objects in the mind is called a hypocrite (3.6).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast are not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (mohakalila, 2.52); delusion (saṃmoha) arises from anger and leads to loss of memory (2.63); one who attains the brāhmī sthiti is not deluded (2.72); desire deludes the embodied one (3.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sage of steady mind is not agitated in sorrows and is free of passion, fear and anger (2.56); the seeing sage is awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: A person does not attain naiṣkarmya by not undertaking actions (3.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument: varṇa-mixture leads family-destroyers and the family to hell (1.42); those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell for an indefinite time, as 'we have heard' (1.44).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Beings follow their own nature; what will suppression accomplish? (3.33).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Objects turn away from the embodied one who does not feed on them, all but the relish (2.59).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is to fight free from expectation and 'mine', having renounced all actions in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).

literal: free from the pairs of opposites

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One of the qualities Arjuna is told to have when free of the three guṇas (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Without the sense of 'mine': the one who attains peace (2.71); Arjuna is to fight nirmama (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: When understanding crosses the thicket of delusion, one reaches nirveda towards what is to be heard and what has been heard (2.52).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The twofold commitment declared by Kṛṣṇa of old: by the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and by the yoga of action for the yogins (3.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of the three guṇas, which are the domain of the Vedas (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.18, 2.20, 2.21, 2.24).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The action Arjuna is told to perform, action being better than inaction (3.8); commentators take niyata as 'prescribed/obligatory'.

notes: The commentators take it as obligatory (daily) rites or one's appointed duty.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wise, who grieve neither for the dead nor for the living (2.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sin: Arjuna fears it would cling to them for killing kin (1.36, 1.39, 1.45); Kṛṣṇa says refusing the dharmic battle incurs it (2.33) while fighting with equanimity does not (2.38); those who cook only for themselves eat sin (agha, 3.13); Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will (3.36).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Another's dharma, even well performed, is worse than one's own deficient dharma and brings danger (3.35).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One is never entitled to the fruits of action (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are pitiable (2.49).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna says that when classes are mixed the ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water (piṇḍodaka-kriyā, 1.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The ancestors, who fall when deprived of the rice-ball and water offerings because of varṇa-mixture (1.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The creator who in the beginning created beings together with sacrifice and told them to prosper by it (3.10).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wisdom that is 'firmly established' in the one who neither rejoices nor hates, withdraws and restrains the senses (2.57, 2.58, 2.61, 2.68); carried away when the mind follows the senses (2.67). Arjuna is said to speak prajñāvāda, words of (seeming) wisdom (2.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇas born of prakṛti make everyone act (3.5); actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); beings deluded by its guṇas are attached to their workings (3.29); one's own nature, which even the knower follows (3.33).

literal: one who has come for refuge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple who has taken refuge in him and asks to be instructed (2.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attained by the disciplined one who moves among objects with senses free of passion and aversion (2.64); in it all sorrows cease and understanding quickly becomes steady (2.65).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The adverse result which is not found in the yoga of understanding (2.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Gone from the sage of steady mind (2.56); senses free of rāga and dveṣa lead to serenity (2.64); set with dveṣa in each sense towards its object, a waylayer (3.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire and anger arise from the guṇa rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The inner taste for sense-objects that remains when one abstains from them and turns away only on seeing the highest (2.59).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In which the resolute understanding of the ritual-minded is not established (2.44); in which understanding must stand immovable for one to attain yoga (2.53); the one of steady wisdom is 'established in samādhi' (2.54). Commentators gloss the word variously in these verses.

notes: Some commentators take samādhi in 2.44 and 2.53 as the mind, or the self, in which one concentrates.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga: being the same in success and failure (2.48); making pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same (2.38); the one who is the same in pain and pleasure is fit for immortality (2.15).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The way in which the understanding of 2.11–38 was declared, contrasted with 'yoga' (2.39); the sāṃkhyas are those whose commitment is the yoga of knowledge (3.3). The chunk does not relate the term to a school.

notes: The commentators divide on how far the Gītā's sāṃkhya relates to the classical Sāṃkhya darśana.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Perfection is not reached by renunciation (saṃnyasana) alone (3.4); Arjuna is to renounce all actions in Kṛṣṇa and fight (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The perfection Janaka and others reached by action (3.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self-restrained, awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.24) and, in Arjuna's argument, of the family dharmas (1.40).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attachment: not to inaction (2.47); to be abandoned in action (2.48, 3.9); arises from dwelling on objects and gives rise to desire (2.62); the ignorant are attached to action and to the actions of the guṇas (3.26, 3.29); the knower is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Without cultivation there is no peace, and without peace no happiness (2.66); the one whom desires enter as rivers the ocean, and who abandons all desires, attains peace (2.70–71).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The embodied one casts off worn-out bodies like clothes (2.22); it is not slain when the body is slain (2.20); without action even the maintenance of the body (śarīrayātrā) is impossible (3.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The eternal, indestructible, immeasurable embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Epithet of the embodied one (2.24) and of brahman established in sacrifice (3.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.16: what is (the existent or real), of which there is no non-being (abhāva); what exactly is meant is disputed among commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In nityasattvastha, 'ever abiding in sattva' (2.45), one of the qualities of being free of the three guṇas.

notes: Taken as the guṇa sattva or as 'being, the real'; the commentators divide.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Success, as against failure, to which one is to be equal (2.48); perfection, not reached by renunciation alone (3.4) but reached by Janaka and others through action (saṃsiddhi, 3.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and asks to be instructed (2.7); Duryodhana calls Dhṛṣṭadyumna Droṇa's disciple (1.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Confusion of memory (smṛtivibhrama) follows delusion, and the loss of memory destroys the understanding (2.63).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna, overwhelmed by grief, casts aside his bow (1.47) and sees nothing that would dispel his grief (2.8); Kṛṣṇa: the wise do not grieve (2.11), and since the embodied one is imperishable and death certain for the born, Arjuna should not grieve (2.25–30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who constantly follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without carping are freed from actions (3.31).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna sees no good in killing kin (1.31), holds living on alms better (2.5), and asks what is better (2.7) and for the one thing by which he may reach the good (3.2); by nourishing one another gods and humans attain the highest good (3.11); one's own dharma is better (3.35); nothing is better for a kṣatriya than a dharmic battle (2.31).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In śrutivipratipannā (2.53): the understanding perplexed by what it has heard, which is to stand immovable in samādhi; cf. nirveda towards what is to be heard and what has been heard (2.52).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Synonym of sthitaprajña in Arjuna's question (2.54); the sage whose mind is unshaken by sorrow and pleasure and free of passion, fear and anger (2.56).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The person described in 2.55–72: gives up all desires that enter the mind, content in the self by the self (2.55); his wisdom is firmly established when he is unattached, withdraws the senses and masters them (2.57–68); his state is the brāhmī sthiti (2.72).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Pleasure and pain come from sense-contacts (2.14) and are to be made the same (2.38); for one without peace there is no happiness (2.66).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One joined with understanding casts off both here (2.50).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna should not waver when he looks to his own dharma as a kṣatriya (2.31); abandoning it incurs sin (2.33); one's own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's well performed, and death in it is better (3.35).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's faintness does not lead to heaven (2.2); a dharmic battle is an open door to heaven (2.32) and heaven is gained if slain (2.37); the Veda-delighters are intent on heaven (2.43).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The seers of truth (tattvadarśibhiḥ) have seen the conclusion (anta) about the real and the unreal (2.16). (The knower of truth at 3.28 is called tattvavit: trm:tattvavid.)
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The knower of the truth about the division of guṇas and actions, who is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to endure (titikṣasva) the impermanent sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The domain of the Vedas (traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ vedāḥ, 2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The social orders whose mixture (varṇa-saṅkara) Arjuna fears (1.41).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument it arises when the women of a family are corrupted after adharma prevails (1.41), leads the family and its destroyers to hell (1.42) and uproots the jāti- and kula-dharmas (1.43); Kṛṣṇa says that if he did not act he would be the maker of saṅkara (3.24).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in the words of the Veda and say there is nothing else proclaim a flowery speech aimed at heaven, enjoyment and power (2.42–44); the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain (2.45); for a knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood (2.46).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in vedavāda say 'there is nothing else' and proclaim flowery speech offering heaven, power and rebirth as fruit of works (2.42–43).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: With jñāna, what desire destroys (3.41); commentators differ on the distinction.

notes: The commentators distinguish jñāna and vijñāna variously.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's condition: overcome by compassion and sinking into despondency (viṣīdan, 1.28, 2.1, 2.10).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense-objects: they turn away from one who abstains, though the taste remains (2.59); dwelling on them breeds attachment (2.62); the self-governed move among them with mastered senses (2.64).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Here it is one, whereas the understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless (2.41); it is not established in samādhi for those carried away by enjoyment and power (2.44).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action other than for the sake of sacrifice binds (3.9); Prajāpati created beings together with sacrifice, by which gods and humans nourish one another (3.10–12); rain arises from sacrifice and sacrifice from action (3.14); the all-pervading brahman is ever established in it (3.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The good who eat the remainder of the sacrifice are freed from all faults (3.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Equanimity is called yoga (2.48); yoga is skill in actions (2.50); the understanding 'according to yoga' (2.39); one attains yoga when the understanding stands immovable in samādhi (2.53); karmayoga is the commitment of the yogins (3.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of concern for acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema) (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.3 the yogins are those whose commitment is the yoga of action.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One should sit disciplined, intent on Kṛṣṇa (2.61); the undisciplined (ayukta) have no understanding or cultivation (2.66); the knowing one acts disciplined (3.26); one joined with understanding (buddhiyukta) casts off good and evil deeds (2.50).
